dimensions.name: Fairness Evaluation — Fair & Representative Training Data Assurance
dimensions.summary:
<scope>
Review the target for defects that make fairness evaluation of educational software incomplete, inconsistent, or misleading. Focus on the representativeness of data used for training, validation, benchmarking, evaluation, or audit; the definition and handling of fairness groups; and whether group-level evaluation can detect failures hidden by aggregate results.
</scope>
<review_standard>
Treat the supplied review target as the scope: it may be a single file, multiple files, a diff/change set, or a broader codebase area. Review any behavior-affecting source, test, schema, configuration, migration, query, prompt/template, data/model artifact, build/deployment file, or UI asset that is relevant to this dimension. Determine intended behavior from repository evidence before judging it. Trace relevant control and data flow through callers, callees, shared utilities, persistence, asynchronous work, and framework/library defaults as needed; do not restrict analysis to the changed lines when surrounding context is necessary. Apply every criterion below to every relevant path, and continue the review after finding an issue rather than stopping at the first plausible bug. The listed evidence signals are examples, not an exhaustive checklist. If a criterion is not applicable to the target, do not force a finding.
</review_standard>
<reporting_bar>
Report every concrete code-level defect or behaviorally meaningful defect you can ground in a reachable input, state, data flow, or execution sequence, including low-severity or uncertain issues; state uncertainty rather than silently dropping a plausible bug. For a diff/change review, a valid finding must be introduced, exposed, or materially worsened by the target; unchanged code may be used as evidence. For a file or codebase review, a valid finding must exist within the requested scope. A finding should explain the trigger and the incorrect or misleading outcome. Pure style or naming preferences, a missing best practice with no failure path, and concerns whose required behavior cannot be established are not findings.
</reporting_bar>

criteria.name: Unrepresentative Dataset Coverage
criteria.details:
<review_goal>
Determine whether data used to train, validate, benchmark, evaluate, or audit learner-affecting behavior fails to cover the intended learner population, educational settings, sources, or case types well enough for the resulting evaluation to support the repository's stated claims.
</review_goal>
<inspect>
Inspect relevant manifests, queries, schemas, source selection, sampling, filtering, deduplication, splits, subgroup labels, coverage summaries, fixtures, benchmark composition, weighting, and aggregation. Look for intended groups or settings that are absent or severely underrepresented, selection logic that unintentionally removes them, leakage or duplication that distorts apparent coverage, or aggregate results that hide known subgroup gaps.
</inspect>
<verification>
Establish the intended population and evaluation purpose from repository code, configuration, tests, schemas, documentation, or product contracts. Trace how records enter and leave the evaluated dataset and check whether stratification, weighting, balancing, coverage assertions, or separate group-level evaluation already handles the apparent gap. A valid finding requires a concrete coverage blind spot that can make an evaluation or claim misleading; dataset size alone is not evidence, and the review should not require collection of attributes the product intentionally cannot or should not collect.
</verification>

criteria.name: Undefined Fairness Evaluation Attributes
criteria.details:
<review_goal>
Check whether attributes or categories used for fairness evaluation are defined and handled consistently enough for reliable subgroup analysis.
</review_goal>
<inspect>
Inspect schemas, enums, category mappings, normalization, aliases, localization, null/unknown handling, joins, derived group fields, filtering, serialization, aggregation, and fallback paths. Look for ambiguous category meaning, inconsistent producer/consumer mappings, records silently dropped from subgroup analysis, distinct groups unintentionally collapsed, or the same value interpreted differently at different stages.
</inspect>
<verification>
Trace each relevant attribute from its source through transformation to the fairness metric or report. Confirm whether a shared schema, normalization layer, or library already enforces the intended semantics. A valid finding requires a concrete way that ambiguity or inconsistent handling can change subgroup membership, metrics, or the repository's stated fairness evaluation. When group data is intentionally unavailable, evaluate the implemented fallback rather than inventing a requirement to collect more sensitive attributes.
</verification>

criteria.name: Missing Group-Wise Fairness Targets
criteria.details:
<review_goal>
Determine whether an evaluation or release check can pass on aggregate performance while a defined learner subgroup violates the fairness target that the repository intends to enforce.
</review_goal>
<inspect>
Inspect metric computation, subgroup aggregation, thresholds, tolerances, assertions, acceptance gates, generated reports, configuration, CI/release checks, and tests. Look for subgroup metrics that are calculated but ignored, pass/fail logic that reads only aggregate values, incorrect group-to-threshold mappings, missing groups caused by default/fallback behavior, or tests that allow a known subgroup failure to pass validation.
</inspect>
<verification>
Establish which groups and targets actually apply from repository evidence, then follow a failing subgroup value through the validation path to determine whether the overall evaluation can still succeed. Check shared evaluators and configuration before concluding a check is absent. A valid finding requires a defined fairness expectation that can be bypassed or masked; do not invent numerical thresholds or require identical outcomes across groups unless the product specifies that policy.
</verification>

dimensions.name: Pedagogy — Adaptive Fairness & Transparent Learner Progression Integrity
dimensions.summary:
<scope>
Review the target for defects that can produce educationally inappropriate learner progression or intervention behavior. Focus on early-warning logic, persistent adverse learner state, hidden progression requirements, and adaptive sequencing or recommendations that can violate explicit pedagogical or learner-state constraints.
</scope>
<review_standard>
Treat the supplied review target as the scope: it may be a single file, multiple files, a diff/change set, or a broader codebase area. criteria.name: Unvalidated Early-Warning Thresholds
criteria.details:
<review_goal>
Check whether early-warning predictions, risk flags, alerts, or interventions can trigger from thresholds, confidence rules, minimum-evidence rules, timing windows, or missing-data defaults that are inconsistent with the validation or operating assumptions encoded by the product.
</review_goal>
<inspect>
Inspect threshold constants and configuration, feature windows, eligibility rules, minimum-observation checks, confidence/calibration gates, default values, missing-data behavior, model/version metadata, cohort rules, and tests. Look for off-by-one or unit errors, thresholds applied to the wrong score/version, alerts emitted before enough evidence exists, stale configuration, missing values that systematically push learners across a threshold, or a fallback path that bypasses the normal gate.
</inspect>
<verification>
Trace a concrete learner state from available evidence through eligibility, scoring, threshold comparison, and resulting action. Verify whether shared configuration, metadata, or downstream logic supplies the apparent guard. A valid finding requires a reachable case where the system acts outside its defined evidence/timing assumptions or uses a threshold differently from its contract. Absence of external research or validation artifacts is not itself a code defect unless the repository explicitly depends on them.
</verification>

criteria.name: Persistent Negative State
criteria.details:
<review_goal>
Determine whether adverse learner state such as a risk flag, penalty, low-confidence classification, restriction, or negative score can persist or compound after the evidence that created it is stale, corrected, superseded, or no longer sufficient.
</review_goal>
<inspect>
Inspect persisted fields, caches, session restoration, event replay, cumulative formulas, recursive scoring, status transitions, expiry/decay/reset rules, recomputation triggers, retries, idempotency, manual corrections, and multi-session tests. Look for stale values reused as fresh input, transitions with no recovery path, duplicate events that compound a penalty, corrected source data that does not invalidate derived state, or an old flag that becomes evidence for a new flag.
</inspect>
<verification>
Follow at least one realistic sequence across multiple updates or sessions and determine whether fresh evidence can clear, reduce, or recompute the adverse state as intended. Check lifecycle hooks and shared state services before reporting. A valid finding requires stale or duplicated adverse state to change later learner treatment without a current valid basis. Persistence that is explicitly required, bounded, and correctly refreshed by the domain rules is not a defect.
</verification>

criteria.name: Hidden Learning Path Requirements
criteria.details:
<review_goal>
Check whether a learner can be blocked, marked incomplete, redirected, or prevented from progressing by a prerequisite, completion rule, lock, deadline, eligibility condition, or required next action that the product fails to communicate accurately at the point of impact.
</review_goal>
<inspect>
Inspect progression calculations, state machines, route or navigation guards, eligibility checks, feature/configuration gates, API errors, UI locked/incomplete states, progress indicators, localization strings, and tests. Look for backend-only requirements with no surfaced reason, UI/backend disagreement about prerequisites, progress displays that omit a required step, generic errors that hide the actionable condition, or stale client state that shows a path as available when it will be rejected.
</inspect>
<verification>
Trace the same blocking condition through enforcement and the final learner-visible state. Verify whether a shared component or another guaranteed layer supplies the reason and next action. A valid finding requires a reachable state where the system's communicated path conflicts with the enforced path or leaves the learner unable to determine how to proceed. Purely internal conditions that never create a learner-visible inconsistency are outside this criterion.
</verification>

criteria.name: Pedagogically Unconstrained Adaptation
criteria.details:
<review_goal>
Determine whether adaptive sequencing, recommendation, routing, tutoring, or intervention logic can choose an educationally invalid action because explicit pedagogical or learner-state constraints represented by the product are not enforced.
</review_goal>
<inspect>
Inspect recommenders, rankers, rules, prompts, score combination, prerequisite graphs, mastery/level state, completion state, course configuration, availability rules, fallback behavior, re-evaluation, overrides, and tests. Look for optimization scores overriding hard prerequisites, stale learner state, invalid or already-completed content being recommended, no valid fallback when top-ranked content is ineligible, or a decision that fails to update after learner state changes.
</inspect>
<verification>
Trace a concrete learner state through the adaptive decision and compare the selected action with explicit constraints in code, configuration, content metadata, or tests. Verify whether another guaranteed layer filters invalid results. A valid finding requires an implemented product constraint to be bypassed, misapplied, or evaluated with stale/incorrect state. The review should not invent pedagogical rules that the repository does not represent.
</verification>

dimensions.name: Decision Fairness — Protected Attribute Governance & Validated Fairness Enforcement
dimensions.summary:
<scope>
Review the target for learner-affecting decision logic that can create unjustified differential treatment through protected attributes or proxies, rely on an unverified fairness mitigation, or fail to enforce the repository's intended separation between restricted fairness attributes and ordinary decision inputs.
</scope>
<review_standard>
Treat the supplied review target as the scope: it may be a single file, multiple files, a diff/change set, or a broader codebase area. Review any behavior-affecting source, test, schema, configuration, migration, query, prompt/template, data/model artifact, build/deployment file, or UI asset that is relevant to this dimension. Pure style or naming preferences, a missing best practice with no failure path, and concerns whose required behavior cannot be established are not findings.
</reporting_bar>

criteria.name: Protected and Proxy-Based Differential Treatment
criteria.details:
<review_goal>
Check whether a protected attribute or a field acting as a close proxy can unjustifiably change ranking, scoring, routing, gating, recommendation, access, support, or another consequential learner outcome for otherwise comparable cases.
</review_goal>
<inspect>
Trace relevant fields through schemas, feature construction, prompts, rules, filters, thresholds, weights, ranking, model inputs, routing, and final actions. Potential proxies can include geography, language, institution, location-derived values, coded labels, or other fields whose use is functionally tied to a protected characteristic in this product. Look for group-specific thresholds, hidden branching, accidental feature inclusion, fallback differences, or proxy values that alter the outcome without the intended policy path.
</inspect>
<verification>
Demonstrate a concrete path from the attribute or proxy to the consequential decision and compare materially similar inputs where that value differs. Establish whether the use is an intended accommodation, fairness correction, legal/product requirement, or other explicitly justified and enforced path. A valid finding requires the field to change treatment without a supported justification; field presence, correlation, or collection for measurement alone is not sufficient.
</verification>

criteria.name: Unvalidated Fairness Mitigations
criteria.details:
<review_goal>
Determine whether a fairness mitigation implemented in code or configuration can fail to address the disparity it is intended to reduce, or can introduce a new regression, because its effect is not validated by the evidence the repository relies on.
</review_goal>
<inspect>
Inspect group-specific thresholds, weighting, sampling, re-ranking, post-processing, routing exceptions, normalization, constraints, feature changes, associated metrics, fixtures, regression tests, and evaluation configuration. Look for a mitigation wired to the wrong group or metric, direction/sign errors, stale thresholds, code paths that bypass the mitigation, tests that only prove execution rather than effect, or available subgroup results that contradict the mitigation's intended behavior.
</inspect>
<verification>
First establish the mitigation's intended target from code, configuration, tests, documentation, or supplied review context. Trace how it affects the relevant decision or metric and compare against available before/after or expected subgroup behavior. A valid finding requires a concrete mismatch between the mitigation's intended effect and its implemented or tested behavior. Do not require a particular mitigation technique or external study when another repository-supported validation path exists.
</verification>

criteria.name: Unenforced Protected-Attribute Separation
criteria.details:
<review_goal>
Check whether attributes that the repository intends to restrict to fairness evaluation, auditing, or another specially authorized purpose are actually prevented from flowing into ordinary learner decision inputs, while remaining available only where their allowed purpose requires them.
</review_goal>
<inspect>
Inspect data models, DTOs, feature builders, prompt/model inputs, queries, pipelines, storage, serializers, allowlists/denylists, permissions, service boundaries, logging, and tests. Look for an evaluation-only field accidentally copied into a general feature object, unrestricted shared records used by both decisioning and auditing, permissions that do not match the intended separation, or refactors that bypass an existing filtering boundary.
</inspect>
<verification>
Establish the intended restriction from repository evidence and trace each relevant field to its actual consumers. Verify separation enforced by executable boundaries such as types, feature allowlists, access controls, serializers, or service interfaces rather than documentation alone. A valid finding requires an intended restriction to be bypassable or broken. Do not assume every protected attribute must be excluded from every decision, and do not require retention of sensitive data where the product intentionally does not collect it.
</verification>

dimensions.name: Inclusion — Cultural & Accessibility Equity in Design and Code
dimensions.summary:
<scope>
Review the target for behavior that can unnecessarily exclude or disadvantage valid users of educational software through culturally narrow data assumptions, exclusionary product language, accessibility defects, or unsupported assumptions about devices, bandwidth, input methods, or location.
</scope>
<review_standard>
Treat the supplied review target as the scope: it may be a single file, multiple files, a diff/change set, or a broader codebase area. Pure style or naming preferences, a missing best practice with no failure path, and concerns whose required behavior cannot be established are not findings.
</reporting_bar>

criteria.name: Culturally Narrow Representations and Validation
criteria.details:
<review_goal>
Determine whether representation, parsing, validation, storage, or formatting logic rejects, corrupts, collapses, or misinterprets valid user data from cultural or locale contexts that the educational product claims to support.
</review_goal>
<inspect>
Inspect regexes, character restrictions, field lengths, enums, normalization, Unicode handling, case conversion, locale selection, name/identity fields, date/time/number/currency/address parsing, language tags, serialization, database constraints, and tests. Look for ASCII-only assumptions, fixed locale formats, lossy normalization, incorrect timezone/locale defaults, rigid identity options where the product supports broader values, or frontend/backend validation disagreement.
</inspect>
<verification>
Produce a concrete valid input or supported locale that is rejected, corrupted, mis-stored, or mapped incorrectly, and trace it through all relevant layers. Check internationalization libraries and downstream normalization before reporting. A valid finding requires a mismatch with the product's supported domain; support for arbitrary worldwide formats is not required when the product explicitly has a narrower scope.
</verification>

criteria.name: Exclusionary Language in Code and UI
criteria.details:
<review_goal>
Check whether behaviorally meaningful or user-facing language in the target stigmatizes, excludes, or misrepresents supported users, or encodes an assumption that causes the product to communicate or behave incorrectly toward them.
</review_goal>
<inspect>
Inspect learner-, educator-, and administrator-facing strings, errors, labels, generated text templates, prompts, exported reports, canonical categories, and identifiers or comments only when they feed generated behavior, public/developer contracts, or product semantics. Look for unnecessarily gendered defaults, one group labeled as the normal/default and others as deviations, deprecated discriminatory terminology, hostile wording, or language/category mappings that lead to incorrect user-visible classification.
</inspect>
<verification>
Evaluate the wording in its actual audience and domain context and trace whether it reaches product behavior or an externally meaningful contract. Check for required quotations, third-party protocol terms, historical fixtures, and neutral technical terminology. A valid finding requires a concrete exclusionary or misleading effect in a supported context; purely private naming/style preferences with no behavioral or user-facing consequence are not findings.
</verification>

criteria.name: Excluding Access Assumptions
criteria.details:
<review_goal>
Determine whether a supported learner or educator flow becomes unusable, inaccessible, or materially degraded because the implementation assumes a particular input method, sensory ability, viewport/device capability, bandwidth level, or location without an equivalent supported path.
</review_goal>
<inspect>
Inspect semantic HTML/component roles, accessible names, labels, form associations, focus order, keyboard operation, pointer-only interactions, ARIA, status/error announcements, color-only meaning, contrast tokens, media alternatives, responsive behavior, zoom/reflow, asset loading, network/offline fallbacks, device capability checks, geolocation gates, and tests. Use the repository's declared accessibility standard when one exists; otherwise evaluate concrete platform semantics and supported user flows rather than inventing a compliance target.
</inspect>
<verification>
Trace a specific supported flow using the affected input method, assistive behavior, device state, network state, or location condition. Verify browser/framework/component-library defaults and shared wrappers before attributing the failure to the target. A valid finding requires a reachable barrier or materially incorrect behavior, such as an unlabeled interactive control, keyboard trap, inaccessible status change, broken supported viewport, or mandatory capability with no supported alternative.
</verification>

dimensions.name: Transparency — Transparent, Explainable, Validated & Human-Supervised AI Decisioning
dimensions.summary:
<scope>
Review the target for AI, statistical, analytics, or algorithmic behavior that users can materially misinterpret or cannot meaningfully supervise. Focus on opaque decision outputs, causal overclaiming, prediction use outside validated scope, one-way consequential decisions, and automation that bypasses safeguards required by the product.
</scope>
<review_standard>
Treat the supplied review target as the scope: it may be a single file, multiple files, a diff/change set, or a broader codebase area. Pure style or naming preferences, a missing best practice with no failure path, and concerns whose required behavior cannot be established are not findings.
</reporting_bar>

criteria.name: Opaque AI Decision Outputs
criteria.details:
<review_goal>
Check whether a learner-, educator-, or administrator-facing AI or algorithmic score, label, placement, flag, recommendation, or action is presented in a way that can materially mislead the user about what it means, why it is being used, or how certain/limited it is under the product's own transparency requirements.
</review_goal>
<inspect>
Trace the output through model/rule execution, response schemas, transformations, generated summaries, UI rendering, explanation fields, confidence/uncertainty metadata, status labels, audit fields, and tests. Look for meaning lost between backend and UI, confidence shown as certainty, an explanation attached to the wrong decision, raw internal values exposed without required interpretation, or limitations/explanations dropped on one path but present on another.
</inspect>
<verification>
Evaluate the final consumed output, not an isolated lower-level return value, and verify whether a guaranteed downstream layer supplies the required context. Establish the transparency expectation from repository/product evidence or from the consequence level encoded by the workflow. A valid finding requires a concrete path where the surfaced output can be materially misread because required meaning, provenance, uncertainty, or limitation information is missing or incorrect. Never require disclosure of chain-of-thought, sensitive internals, or proprietary model details.
</verification>

criteria.name: Causal Overclaiming in Analytics
criteria.details:
<review_goal>
Determine whether the product presents observational, correlational, predictive, or descriptive analytics as a causal explanation of learner outcomes when the underlying implementation does not support that claim.
</review_goal>
<inspect>
Inspect metric definitions, statistical calculations, chart titles, labels, tooltips, annotations, reports, generated summaries, prompt/templates that produce analytics copy, API fields whose names surface to users, and tests. Look for correlation or feature importance rendered as cause, risk scores explained as reasons, certainty language introduced after a transformation, or a disclaimer present in one channel but omitted in another.
</inspect>
<verification>
Trace the surfaced claim back to the computation and determine what kind of inference the implementation actually supports. Check whether the repository contains an experimental, causal, or otherwise valid design justifying the language. A valid finding requires a user- or decision-facing causal claim that is stronger than the underlying evidence. Internal variable names alone are not findings unless they drive surfaced language or behavior.
</verification>

criteria.name: Mismatched Prediction Validation and Use
criteria.details:
<review_goal>
Check whether a prediction, risk score, classifier, or similar validated decision component is used for a population, outcome, timing window, feature definition, threshold, or decision purpose that differs materially from the scope represented by its repository validation or configuration.
</review_goal>
<inspect>
Inspect model and configuration metadata, feature pipelines, population/cohort filters, label definitions, versions, serving routes, thresholds, call sites, UI actions, fallbacks, and tests. Look for version/config skew, a model reused by a new caller with different semantics, changed label meaning, out-of-scope population routing, thresholds copied from another use case, or preprocessing differences between evaluation and serving.
</inspect>
<verification>
Establish both the validated/declared scope and the actual use from code, configuration, tests, or supplied model documentation, then trace a concrete request across the mismatch. A valid finding requires the implementation to permit materially different use without a corresponding supported validation/configuration path. If the validated scope cannot be established from available evidence, state that limitation rather than guessing it.
</verification>

criteria.name: Unidirectional Algorithmic Decisions Without Educator Contestability
criteria.details:
<review_goal>
Determine whether a consequential algorithmic decision can affect a learner while the authorized human actors defined by the product have no effective way to provide correcting context, contest an incorrect result, request review, or have an accepted correction influence the decision state.
</review_goal>
<inspect>
Inspect feedback/appeal flows, override APIs, reviewer queues, permissions, human-context fields, persistence, audit logs, event routing, recomputation, state transitions, UI states, and tests. Look for controls that exist only visually, feedback that is stored but never consumed, an override that is later overwritten by recomputation, missing authorization on correction paths, or a review request that cannot change the consequential state.
</inspect>
<verification>
First establish that the output is consequential and that the product provides or requires contestability for the relevant actor. Trace a concrete correction or appeal from submission through persistence to downstream behavior and check alternate review paths. A valid finding requires the implemented contestability path to be absent when required, unreachable, ineffective, or inconsistent. Purely informational outputs do not require a contestability mechanism unless the repository says otherwise.
</verification>

criteria.name: Automation Without Review Safeguards
criteria.details:
<review_goal>
Check whether a consequential learner-affecting action can execute automatically while bypassing an approval, permission, override, reversal, or other human-review safeguard that the product requires for that action.
</review_goal>
<inspect>
Inspect handlers, jobs, queues, workflows/state machines, role and permission checks, approval states, feature flags, retries, race conditions, scheduled actions, rollback/reversal paths, audit logs, and tests. Look for execution before approval commits, stale approval reused after inputs change, alternate endpoints/jobs that bypass the gate, unauthorized actors able to approve/override, retry paths that duplicate a consequential action, or reversal that does not restore dependent state.
</inspect>
<verification>
Establish the action's consequence and the applicable safeguard from repository/product evidence, then trace a concrete path to execution. Check upstream and downstream enforcement as well as concurrency/retry behavior before reporting. A valid finding requires an applicable safeguard to be bypassed, incorrectly enforced, or ineffective. Low-impact automation that the product explicitly permits to run autonomously is outside this criterion.
</verification>

dimensions.name: Privacy
dimensions.summary:
<scope>
Review the target for consent-dependent processing of learner personal or educational data that can occur without valid current consent or continue after consent is withdrawn or expires. Apply this dimension only where the repository, product policy, or supplied requirements make consent a prerequisite for the specific processing purpose.
</scope>
<review_standard>
Treat the supplied review target as the scope: it may be a single file, multiple files, a diff/change set, or a broader codebase area. For a file or codebase review, a valid finding must exist within the requested scope. A finding should explain the trigger and the incorrect or misleading outcome. Pure style or naming preferences, a missing best practice with no failure path, and concerns whose required behavior cannot be established are not findings.
</reporting_bar>

criteria.name: Missing Consent Checks for Learner Data
criteria.details:
<review_goal>
Determine whether learner personal or educational data can be collected, used, retained for a processing purpose, or shared on a consent-dependent path without verifying valid current consent, or can continue through that path after consent is withdrawn or expires.
</review_goal>
<inspect>
Inspect collection/UI entry points, APIs, services, middleware/policy layers, jobs and queues, consent records, purpose/scope fields, status and expiry handling, caches, revocation events, retries, third-party transfers, derived-data processing, and tests. Look for missing checks, checks against the wrong learner or purpose, stale cached consent, granted/revoked state races, queued work that ignores a later withdrawal, retries that resurrect cancelled processing, or one consumer that bypasses centralized enforcement.
</inspect>
<verification>
First establish from repository code, configuration, product policy, or supplied requirements that the specific processing purpose is consent-dependent. Trace at least one realistic consent transition, such as granted to revoked or active to expired, through synchronous and asynchronous consumers. Verify centralized enforcement before reporting. A valid finding requires a reachable processing path that operates without the consent state required for that purpose; absence of duplicated checks in every caller is not a defect when a verified central policy enforces them.
</verification>
